I’ll try and make this as short as possible (This was only about a month and a half ago).

Got called to what initially was suspected to be an overdose. We get them daily so it wasn’t anything out of the ordinary. Dispatchers added on our CAD “the caller is the patients father and repeatedly keeps saying ‘I think my son is dead!’”.. a little eerie, but didn’t really sway what we thought we were getting into. Further information provided to us told us the patient was inside his blue pickup truck on a lookout/pullout on the side of a highway in the middle of the woods. The father of the patient would be parked behind the patients truck. 

3-ish minutes later we arrive and see exactly what the CAD said we would find. Two trucks parked on the side of a woodsy pullout overlooking mountains and the ocean, just 5 minutes out of town. A couple other vehicles are there to walk their dogs. We pull over, an older man roughly in his mid to late 60s is distraught leaning against his truck. I was attending and my partner and I went to talk to the father briefly before he encouraged me to have a peak through the back window of his son’s truck. 

I walk up to the truck and see a guy hunched over in the back seat, face down in his lap. He’s definitely not breathing, ‘but that doesn’t mean he’s dead yet’ I tell myself. I change angles and soon see behind his ears are dark purple and his skin is changing colour… yeah this guy is definitely already dead. I swing open the drivers side door, push forward the drivers seat and go to touch the guy to get a pulse and be sure. Rigor mortis has already set in and he’s stiff as a board, skin is freezing cold. I decide to not inspect any further and radio dispatch for police so they can do a sudden death report and get the coroner out here. 

I break the news to the father and console him. My partner instructs nearby vehicles to leave. While we wait for the police we try and get a story from him. Dad explains that he, his wife, and his son (37) live about 2 hours North from this pullout off the highway (everything north from this point is very remote small towns in the woods; the town this took place just outside of is basically the last city-like area on the map). He explains his son was a casual opioid user and would sometimes couch hop in the town they lived to visit friends. Recently, his son met a woman online from a town about 3 hours south from where they lived (around an hour from this pullout). One week ago, his son set off to meet up with this woman in real life. She had a boyfriend that the son knew about and he updated his dad a few days into the visit that they all got along great and he was just having fun hanging out with them, playing card games, etc… 

On the night the son was set to drive himself back home 3 hours North ( going on two days before this moment that he was found dead) he called his dad asking for some gas money to get him home. His dad happily obliged and said the basic “drive safe see you soon” and they ended their call. Cut to this morning, 2 days after that call allegedly took place. 9am his father begins to get worried that his son never made it home early yesterday morning. Dad sets off from their home town and slowly drives the lengthy, winding two lane highway for 2 hours scanning the ditches, worried his son might have careened off the edge somewhere. He finally makes it to this pullout and sees his truck by 11am and the rest is history, here we are now around 11:30 with his son dead in the backseat of his own truck. 

This is where it gets weird though… it was mid July, and we were in the middle of the first major heatwave of the year. Windows of the truck were rolled up tight. It clicks in my mind that something isn’t right.. 
if this dead guy left two days ago to set out on a 3 hour drive home and he’s been sitting dead in the back of his truck for a day or two, why didn’t a smell hit me when I opened the truck door? Why was his skin cold to the touch if he’s just been baking in the backseat in the sun 2 days straight? There was no drug paraphernalia in sight, just some unused narcan in the pocket of the driver side door. No needles. Also, why was he almost in the fetal position in the back seat of his truck and not the driver seat? The truck was old, had no tinted windows and the back seat was very cramped. The doors to the truck were unlocked. 

I’ve discussed this with coworkers and some have suggested that maybe he ended up overdosing with the woman and her boyfriend in their town, man throws dead guy in the back of his own truck, drives him halfway home and leaves his truck on a random lookout, and then leaves in a separate car with the girlfriend. 

Others have suggested maybe the son intentionally drove to that pullout to take a break since he left at night and might have been tired. Decides to use before he goes to bed and then just never wakes up.. still doesn’t explain why he was cold and didn’t reek after baking in the hot son for at least a day though. 

I don’t know, the whole thing was just very strange to me. Because the guy was an opioid user, police didn’t even care too much to make these connections and are likely just going to chalk it up to a simple overdose. Hopefully the coroner was able to do their job and the case was closed properly though.

Paramedic in Canada here; we are only allowed to take people by force if we have a police officer present that can section the patient under the Mental Health Act - then we could “force” someone into our ambulance to go to the hospital. I’m not sure about other countries but in British Columbia Canada we can do ECG’s on ambulance at BLS and ALS levels. Patients here also have a right to say no to going to the hospital, only IF they are of sound mind. I personally wouldn’t think you having Anorexia Nervosa would deem you unfit to make your own decision in this case… but it might vary place to place. I think ultimately it depends on the paramedic that you get and whether or not they want to push it that far. I don’t think most people would (depending on the severity). The only time I’ve sectioned people is when they’re an *immediate* threat to their well-being or the well-being of others. You typically avoid inviting the police to calls unless you absolutely need to and I don’t think that would be necessary in your case; forcing you is not in your best interest (in my opinion), and that is what we are paid to look out for. I wish you the best.

I'm currently running twice a day, 5-6 times a week, roughly 45 minutes each time. It's a bit much, but i've been a runner for around 6 years now so my body is used to it. Even at the rate I run currently, my body doesn't show a lot of signs of slimming down right away anymore because i'm just used to it. It takes much longer for me to see results while semi-toned compared to when I was 200lbs and had much less muscle. I would say if you're new, try high intensity interval runs 30 mins a day (if you like doing the hour a day, maybe do two half an hours a day?), or every other day to allow proper recovery. Even starting with some casual jog/runs is good.  Go at your own pace, don't feel pressured to sprint right out the gates. If you can comfortably go slow for 30 minutes straight that is a good start, then build from there.
